title: Very High Cycle Fatigue of Wrought NiTi Shape Memory Alloys
abstract: Abstract Very-high-cycle fatigue (VHCF) data for superelastic NiTi beyond 10 7  cycles remain limited, particularly for wrought, precipitate-tuned conditions tested under ultrasonic loading. Here, the VHCF response of a Ni-rich wrought NiTi (Ni50.8Ti49.2) was quantified by coupling calorimetry and monotonic mechanics with 20 kHz axial ultrasonic fatigue in fully reversed loading (R =  − 1) using pulse-pause control and forced-air cooling to mitigate self-heating. The alloy was solutionized at 1000 °C for 2 h and aged at 600 °C for 1 h to promote Ni4Ti3 precipitation. DSC showed suppressed transformation temperatures relative to the non-heat-treated state, with a two-step B2 → R → B19′ sequence on cooling and a sharp reverse transformation on heating (A f  = 9–10 °C). Room-temperature tensile tests confirmed a fully austenitic starting state (E = 61.9 GPa) and a stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) onset near 223 MPa with a 250–300 MPa transformation plateau. S–N data spanning 10 5  to 10 9  cycles were fitted by a Basquin relation (σ f ’ = 653.7 MPa, b =  − 0.089), indicating a gradual fatigue-strength reduction with increasing life and increased scatter in the VHCF regime without a clear endurance limit. Fractography and EDS revealed a stress-dependent transition in crack initiation: higher-amplitude failures were dominated by surface slip/damage, whereas VHCF failures initiated subsurface at Ti − rich non-metallic inclusions (TiC and Ti2NiOx). These results provide a benchmark VHCF dataset for wrought NiTi under R =  − 1 ultrasonic loading and clarify how precipitation-tuned transformation behavior and inclusion populations govern VHCF crack initiation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Over the past two decades, some studies [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ] have examined the fatigue behavior of superelastic NiTi under conventional frequencies (typical servo-hydraulic testing), revealing that fatigue life is influenced by factors such as microstructure, surface quality, inclusions, mean strain, and environmental conditions. For instance, non-metallic inclusions (e.g., TiC, Ti2NiOx) are frequently cited as fatigue crack initiation sites in NiTi [ 4 ,  5 ]. Higher inclusion content or larger inclusion size has been correlated with reduced fatigue life [ 6 ,  7 ], and modeling approaches have been proposed to predict fatigue strength from inclusion-size distributions [ 8 ,  9 ]. Surface conditions are likewise critical; surface defects or roughness can dramatically reduce fatigue life, while improvements such as electropolishing can enhance it [ 10 ]. The material's thermomechanical processing history significantly influences its properties, particularly phase transformations and the martensite-to-austenite transformation. For instance, cold work can modify the fatigue performance of NiTi wires. At the same time, excessive pre-strains, resulting from device deployment or shape-setting, may either diminish fatigue life or, in certain instances, enhance it by promoting advantageous microstructural alterations [ 11 ,  12 ].

High-cycle fatigue (HCF, 10 4 –10 7  cycles) of superelastic NiTi has been widely investigated because most service conditions for biomedical wires/tubes and actuators fall within this regime, and because the fatigue response is strongly coupled with stress-induced phase transformation. Prior work has consistently shown that fatigue performance is primarily governed by (i) crack initiation from inclusions/defects or surface damage, and (ii) transformation-assisted cyclic inelasticity rather than classical slip-only mechanisms. For example, structural/functional fatigue concepts specific to SMAs were consolidated by Eggeler et al. [ 1 ]. At the same time, Robertson and Ritchie [ 13 ,  14 ] demonstrated that fatigue crack growth/fracture behavior in superelastic NiTi tubing provides a basis for defect tolerance in stent-like components. Mechanistically, Gall and Maier [ 15 ] linked cyclic deformation in precipitated NiTi to transformation-related microstructural evolution (and the resulting local accumulation of damage). Processing/surface-state outcomes are also evident in HCF: cold-work level and surface finish can significantly affect fatigue life by altering the density of micro-notches and the probability of surface-initiated cracking [ 10 ,  11 ]. More recent studies emphasize that HCF deformation mechanisms in NiTi involve a transformation-plasticity interplay that can modify cyclic stability and damage accumulation with life [ 2 ,  16 ,  17 ]. Collectively, these HCF findings establish that surface quality, inclusion population, and transformation characteristics jointly govern the transition from surface-dominated to defect-dominated fatigue, thereby motivating the extension of the dataset into the VHCF regime.

Given the central role of NiTi SMAs in long-life, safety–critical components, a mechanistic understanding of damage evolution in the VHCF regime remains essential yet incomplete. Despite progress, three gaps persist: (i) a scarcity of wrought, precipitate-tuned NiTi datasets that extend to VHCFs under instrumented ultrasonic loading; (ii) an incomplete linkage between the thermodynamics/kinetics of the B2 → R → B19′ transformation pathway (as tuned by Ni₄Ti₃ precipitation) and the transition from surface-controlled to inclusion-controlled crack initiation across the HCF → VHCF regimes; and (iii) limited, chemically resolved evidence identifying which inclusion species (e.g., TiC vs.Ti 2 NiO x ) are life-limiting at low stress amplitudes, along with ongoing uncertainty regarding any practical endurance limit at VHCFs. This study aims to establish a consistent, microstructure-based framework for VHCF of wrought NiTi by coupling calorimetry and monotonic mechanics with ultrasonic fatigue and fractography. The specific objectives are to: (1) determine the VHCF S–N response to fully reversed loading (R =  − 1) using 20 kHz pulse-pause testing with forced-air cooling, and extract Basquin-law parameters; (2) understand the correlation between the phase transformation behavior and fatigue performance of NiTi SMAs; and (3) examine the mechanisms of crack initiation and propagation in NiTi under USF conditions. The novelty of this study lies in employing USF testing to investigate the VHCF behavior of fabricated NiTi SMAs and to establish a direct link between phase transformation characteristics and fatigue response. By integrating thermal treatments to control precipitate formation (particularly Ni₄Ti₃) and by characterizing carbides and other secondary phases on the fracture surface, this work provides new insights into how transformation pathways and microstructural heterogeneities govern crack initiation and propagation mechanisms under gigacyclic loading. The approach enables the correlation of transformation-induced stress accommodation and precipitate distribution with the observed fatigue life and fracture morphology.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
The Effect of HT on Microstructure
paragraphs: In addition to the temperature shifts, the DSC curve shape indicates alterations in the sharpness and sequence of transformations. The non-HT sample exhibits a pervasive one-step martensitic transformation, characterized by a unique smooth exothermic peak during cooling and an endothermic peak during heating, indicating a direct B2 (austenite) to B19′ (martensite) phase transition. In the HT sample, the peaks exhibit greater and a multi-stage structure. The cooling DSC curve of the HT sample shows a two-step transformation: a minor first peak followed by a larger peak, indicating the presence of the R-phase before the martensite transformation. The transformation sequence has shifted from a single-stage process in the non-HT sample to a two-stage process following aging treatment. This is a well-known effect in Ni-rich NiTi, aging induces an intermediate R-phase (rhombohedral phase) between austenite and martensite [ 32 ]. The cooling curve of the HT sample exhibits an initial exotherm at elevated temperatures (beginning about –10 to –20 °C) before the main martensitic exotherm occurring around –30 to –40 °C, demonstrating the B2 to R-phase transition followed by the R to B19' transformation. Upon heating, both cycles of the HT sample exhibit a single endothermic peak, indicating that martensite transforms directly to austenite. The R-phase formed during cooling is not retained after reheating; it reverts to austenite nearly simultaneously with the martensite transformation, resulting in a single peak. This pattern (two-step during cooling, one-step during heating) aligns with published findings for aged Ni-rich NiTi [ 33 ].

sections.heading: Tensile Properties
paragraphs: Although both specimens exhibit this general topology, there are subtle yet significant distinctions. Sample 1 exhibits slightly higher transformation stress and a longer plateau before transitioning to strain hardening, ultimately reaching a higher UTS (654 MPa). Sample 2 shows earlier deviation from the plateau and a lower work-hardening rate in the high-strain regime. Such divergence between nominally identical, polished specimens is standard in NiTi. It is typically traced to mesoscale heterogeneity: (i) spatial variations in Ni 4 Ti 4  size/number density and their associated coherency fields, which bias variant selection and R-phase participation; (ii) slight differences in inclusion population (TiC, Ti 2 NiO x , oxide/nitride) and surface-adjacent defects that act as local stress intensification areas and early SIMT saturation sites; and (iii) weak crystallographic texture and grain-scale constraint effects that alter the ease of variant reorientation [ 4 ,  9 ]. A longer plateau in Sample 1 implies a more spatially uniform SIMT front with delayed activation of irreversible slip. In contrast, the earlier hardening in Sample 2 suggests more rapid local saturation of transformable variants and earlier crossover to dislocation plasticity. The higher UTS of Sample 1 is consistent with a microstructure that resists slip accumulation to larger strains. In contrast, Sample 2 likely accommodates more strain by mixed SIMT–slip from an earlier stage [ 35 ,  36 ].

These tensile features are essential for ultrasonic VHCF testing and aid in interpreting long-life damage mechanisms. First, the measured modulus and density were used to tune the USF resonant geometry, ensuring that the targeted stress amplitudes fall within the SIMT-dominated regime rather than deep into plasticity, which is critical for isolating transformation-controlled dissipation from slip-controlled ratcheting at 20 kHz. Second, because the transformation stress scales with T-A s  (Clausius-Clapeyron), the lowered A s /A f  after aging directly explains the moderate plateau stresses we observe at room temperature; this, in turn, implies that at the same stress amplitude, the fraction of the gauge undergoing reversible SIMT is appreciable, increasing cyclic latent-heat exchange but, with pulse-pause and forced air, remaining compatible with quasi-isothermal testing. Third, specimen-to-specimen differences in plateau length and the strain at which hardening begins are well-known predictors of fatigue scatter in NiTi: microstructures that preserve a long, uniform SIMT plateau tend to delay the onset of localized plasticity, which is strongly linked to crack-nucleating damage at inclusions or at surface asperities [ 1 ,  2 ]. Conversely, earlier hardening concentrates plastic shear around inclusions and precipitate clusters, which could accelerate the formation of micro-cracks under VHCF regime, as widely reported in long-life NiTi and in steels tested in VHCFs [ 13 ,  25 ].

sections.heading: Fatigue Response
paragraphs: Data scatter across HCF/VHCF is attributable to variability in crack initiation sites, microstructural heterogeneities, and thermal/loading effects. Although transformation hysteresis governs cyclic dissipation in NiTi, the DSC hysteresis reported here (30–33 °C for the heat-treated condition) represents a bulk response and was not measured for each fatigued specimen; thus, the present dataset does not support a statistical correlation between VHCF life scatter and specimen-to-specimen hysteresis variations. The increased scatter in the VHCF regime is more consistently attributed to the transition to inclusion-controlled crack initiation, as verified by SEM/EDS. In contrast, unmeasured small temperature fluctuations during ultrasonic cycling may contribute secondarily by modulating the local transformation fraction. At higher stresses (HCF), cracks likely initiate at the specimen surface (e.g., from surface slip bands or minor surface defects as illustrated in the fractography section of this paper). In contrast, at lower stress amplitudes (in the VHCF domain), failure may sometimes initiate in the subsurface (e.g., at an internal flaw or a weak microstructural site) [ 38 ]. This mix of surface  vs.  interior initiation mechanisms can produce a wide lifetime scattering in VHCF. On the other hand, even with identical heat treatment, slight variations in microstructure (precipitate distribution, grain orientation, etc.) can lead to differences in the mechanisms and timing of fatigue crack initiation in the VHCF regime. The effect of self-heating on phase transformation during the fatigue test is another possibility correlated with NiTi properties.

The present HCF → VHCF response (gradual loss of fatigue strength with increasing scatter and no clear endurance limit) is consistent with prior long-life fatigue studies of superelastic Nitinol in which the dominant crack-initiation mechanism transitions from surface-driven to defect/inclusion-controlled as the cyclic driving force decreases. In particular, ultrasonic-frequency experiments combined with in situ synchrotron measurements have shown that the cyclic response of superelastic Nitinol can be sensitive to strain-rate/thermal conditions and may exhibit evolving strain partitioning and damage localization during VHCF loading, supporting the need to interpret Basquin parameters as empirical descriptors tied to the applied boundary conditions rather than universal constants [ 4 ,  28 ]. Beyond ultrasonic testing, ultra-high-cycle rotary-bend/bending datasets to 10 8 -10 9  cycles similarly report increasing life scatter and inclusion-governed initiation at very long lives, often associated with a smooth origin region surrounding the initiating inclusion features that qualitatively align with the inclusion-initiated morphologies documented in the present fractography/EDS observations [ 22 ,  27 ,  39 ].

A direct, point-to-point quantitative comparison between the present wrought, precipitate-tuned NiTi and AM NiTi under identical ultrasonic loading (axial 20 kHz, fully reversed R =  − 1, comparable specimen geometry/surface finish, and equivalent thermal management) is currently limited by the scarcity of published datasets that match these boundary conditions. The closest ultrasonic VHCF study on AM Nitinol identified in the recent literature employed ultrasonic loading up to the VHCF regime but introduced a superimposed compressive mean load to control transformation fraction, which makes the mean-stress state fundamentally different from the fully reversed condition used here and therefore prevents an apples-to-apples comparison of Basquin parameters or endurance levels. Nevertheless, the present dataset provides a quantitative benchmark for dense wrought NiTi under R =  − 1 ultrasonic loading: failures span from 10 5  cycles at high stress amplitudes (e.g., 245–268 MPa giving 1.0–1.9 × 10 5  cycles) to the VHCF regime (e.g., 128 MPa giving 1.8 × 10 8  cycles), and the fitted power-law offers a reference for future head-to-head AM vs wrought campaigns conducted under matched ultrasonic conditions. (A dedicated one-to-one experimental comparison using AM NiTi specimens produced and finished with comparable surface quality and tested under identical pulse-pause thermal control is planned as future work.)

The experiments were conducted in ultrasonic pulse-pause mode to reduce self-heating. However, the material's local fatigue behavior may be influenced by minor temperature increases or environmental variations, particularly given that NiTi's properties are temperature sensitive. The absence of precise temperature control and measurement means that minor thermal fluctuations may contribute to the scatter in cycles, leading to failure. According to the theory [ 40 ,  41 ], greater self-heating is observed at elevated stress levels (20 kHz) than at reduced stress levels. Consequently, the material will undergo increased heating during testing at elevated stress levels. Although the A f  for the heat-treated samples is approximately 10, and the entire sample is in the austenite phase at room temperature under the testing conditions, self-heating phenomena could still affect residual martensite phases in the samples or even affect the R-phases (rhombohedral phase).

At first glance, the runout stress amplitude (100 MPa) may appear low relative to the VHCF fatigue strengths reported for some high-strength structural alloys; however, direct cross-material comparisons based solely on stress amplitude can be misleading. In high-strength steels, VHCF strengths are often reported to be on the order of 50% of UTS, although internal inclusion-driven failure beyond 10⁷ cycles is common in the VHCF regime [ 42 ]. In titanium alloys, values can be substantially higher when defects are minimized; for example, HIPed LPBF Ti6Al4V exhibits σ max  = 483 ± 16 MPa at 10 9  cycles under fully reversed loading [ 43 ]. Conversely, under the same 20 kHz ultrasonic, R =  − 1 framework used here, markedly lower VHCF strengths are also reported for defect- and surface-sensitive states, such as as-built SLM Ti6Al4V (90–100 MPa) and polished Ti6Al4V (120–140 MPa) between 10⁶-10⁹ cycles [ 44 ], and notched AW7075 showing 93–107 MPa at 10 9  cycles [ 45 ]. For NiTi specifically, stress-based comparisons should also be interpreted in light of its lower elastic modulus (one-third of steel), such that σ a  ≈ 100 MPa corresponds to an elastic strain amplitude of only 0.14%. In the present study, the runout domain remains below the SIMT start stress, so deformation is dominated by elastic austenite, and the practical VHCF threshold is governed by defect-assisted microcrack nucleation rather than by macroplasticity-driven HCF mechanisms.

The quantitative stress-life parameters reported here (Basquin coefficients, transition stress, and scatter magnitude) are specific to the present wrought NiTi condition (solutionized + aged) because VHCF behavior in NiTi depends strongly on the position of A f  relative to the test temperature, on the Ni 4 Ti 3  precipitation state (which controls transformation stresses and slip resistance), and on matrix Ni content (which governs transformation temperatures and precipitation kinetics). However, two qualitative outcomes are expected to be broadly transferable across NiTi conditions: (i) a transition toward defect/inclusion-controlled subsurface initiation in VHCF as cyclic driving force decreases, and (ii) the governing role of rare, life-limiting defects in controlling VHCF scatter. Quantitative transfer to other compositions/aging states requires calibration under matched temperature and loading conditions.

The fatigue behavior must be interpreted in the context of the alloy’s microstructure and phase transformation characteristics. All specimens were solutionized and aged, a treatment known to precipitate fine Ni 4 Ti 3  particles throughout the NiTi matrix. This precipitation hardens the austenite and significantly influences the martensitic transformation behavior. DSC results (presented earlier) likely indicate modifications to the phase transformation, for example, the appearance of an intermediate R-phase and altered martensitic start/finish temperatures due to Ni depletion in the matrix via Ni 4 Ti 3  formation [ 31 ]. In tensile tests, the aged NiTi exhibited a pronounced SIMT plateau, occurring at a relatively high stress level because Ni₄Ti₃ precipitates increase the critical transformation stress (precipitation creates coherency strains and reduces matrix Ni content, which typically raises the austenite’s resistance to transformation, thereby requiring higher stress to initiate martensite).

Crucially, the role of stress-induced phase transformation distinguishes NiTi’s fatigue response from that of conventional metals. Under cyclic loading, if the stress amplitude exceeds the austenite-to-martensite transformation start stress, the material undergoes a hysteretic phase transformation in each cycle [ 19 ,  28 ]. Each tensile half-cycle (reversal) transforms austenite into martensite (manifested as the flat plateau in the stress–strain curve), and each unloading allows martensite to revert to austenite. This cyclic phase change dissipates energy (reducing the effective stress experienced by the material) and induces microstructural damage over time. Internally, repeated martensitic transformation can create dislocations and defects where incompatibilities at austenite/martensite interfaces or around Ni 4 Ti 3  precipitates lead to local plasticity that accumulates cycle by cycle. Eventually, this localized damage can nucleate a fatigue crack. Notably, Ni 4 Ti 3  precipitates may serve as sites of stress concentration in this context. The fracturing of the matrix at or near such sites could be an early crack-initiation mechanism, particularly in the VHCF regime, when numerous transformation cycles have occurred. On the other hand, the precipitates also increase overall fatigue resistance by raising the transformation stress and strengthening the matrix [ 31 ,  32 ,  34 ]. This dual effect is reflected in our results: high fatigue strength (due to a high transformation plateau stress) but considerable life scatter (since microscale interactions between transforming matrix and precipitates can vary from site to site).

sections.heading: Fractography Assessments
paragraphs: For clarity, Fig.  6  presents representative fracture surfaces; however, the same SEM-based initiation-site identification procedure was applied to the failed specimens to classify initiation as surface-dominated versus inclusion-dominated. This work identifies life-limiting crack-origin inclusions using SEM/EDS fractography, but it does not provide quantitative statistics on the bulk inclusion population. A meticulous inclusion size distribution and extreme value analysis (EVA) (which is particularly relevant for VHCF, where the maximum defect within the stressed volume governs failure probability) was outside the scope of the present dataset and would require systematic metallographic/BSE imaging across statistically meaningful areas/volumes and subsequent EVA of the largest-inclusion distribution.

The fracture surface (in Fig.  6 a) is rough and uneven, indicating significant cyclic plasticity before final failure. Crack initiation occurred at the surface, as evidenced by the origin located at the specimen edge (region 1 in Fig.  6 a). The local fracture morphology near this origin shows microvoid coalescence and tearing, suggesting a relatively ductile fracture process once the crack formed. No prominent singular inclusion is apparent at the initiation site for this high-stress sample; correspondingly, EDS of region 1 detects mainly the matrix elements Ni (~ 50 wt%) and Ti (~ 45 wt%) with only minor light elements (a few wt.% C and O). This implies the crack nucleated from a surface weakness (such as a minor surface defect or intense slip band) rather than a prominent defect particle like an inclusion or precipitate. However, small oxide/carbide particles may still be involved; EDS did pick up modest carbon and oxygen signals in some micro-regions around the origin (on the order of 10–20 wt% each, with Ni and Ti depleted). This suggests a finely dispersed non-metallic inclusion or surface contamination was present. Such inclusions are most likely Ti–rich (given the low local Ni content) and could correspond to oxidic or carbide phases. Indeed, NiTi is known to contain titanium carbides (TiC) and titanium oxides (Ti 2 NiO x ) as trace inclusions from processing. In this specimen, any inclusion at the origin was small enough that the fracture still appears dominated by ductile transgranular features. Once the crack nucleated, it propagated rapidly, as indicated by the extensive radial shear zones and final overload dimples toward the opposite side of the fracture. The overall behavior at 80% reflects a high stress amplitude regime where stress-induced martensitic transformation SIMT would occur each cycle, contributing to localized plasticity at the surface that facilitates crack nucleation. The result is a surface-initiated fatigue failure, with a fracture morphology exhibiting significant plastic deformation.

Since EDS was performed post-mortem on fracture surfaces, oxygen detected at crack-origin regions can reflect either (i) pre-existing oxide-bearing inclusions (e.g., Ti₂NiOx) or (ii) oxidation after the crack becomes surface-connected and/or after final fracture. In the present specimens, oxygen enrichment is highly localized and accompanied by Ni depletion and/or strong carbon-rich signatures, consistent with Ti 2 NiO x - and TiC-type inclusions at the initiation site, supporting an inclusion-controlled initiation mechanism. Moreover, for subsurface initiation, the life-dominating initiation stage occurs before surface breakthrough, limiting direct environmental access to the origin. Nonetheless, a contribution from post-fracture oxidation cannot be entirely excluded; future work will use site-specific cross-sectioning (FIB/SEM with EDS mapping) and/or inert-atmosphere ultrasonic testing to decouple intrinsic inclusion chemistry from any oxidation acquired after crack opening.

The current heat treatment (solutionizing at 1000 °C followed by aging at 600 °C) was selected to form Ni₄Ti₃ precipitates before fatigue testing. Although Ni 4 Ti 3  strongly affects transformation pathways and cyclic response, the current study did not include quantitative precipitate metrology (TEM-based size/number density/volume fraction, or coherency measurements) before and after fatigue. Consequently, we cannot directly report on how Ni₄Ti₃ evolves over 10 8 - 10 9  cycles. Nevertheless, diffusion-controlled changes in precipitate size or volume fraction are expected to be negligible under the present room-temperature USF conditions because Ni 4 Ti 4  precipitation/coarsening is governed primarily by thermal aging kinetics rather than mechanical cycling at ambient temperature [ 31 ,  34 ]. By contrast, the more plausible evolution during long-life cycling is mechanically driven relaxation of local coherency fields and transformation-assisted defect accumulation in the matrix near precipitates, particularly where SIMT is locally activated. This view aligns with cyclic-deformation studies of precipitate-strengthened NiTi and with recent reports emphasizing that beneficial precipitate effects can be compromised once precipitates lose coherency and promote inelastic deformation [ 46 ,  47 ]. Future work will quantify precipitate size distributions and coherency before/after VHCF via targeted TEM (and/or scattering methods) on the fatigued gauge volume to directly link precipitate stability to gigacyclic lifetime.

The lowest-stress specimen exhibits a distinctly different failure mode, initiated by an internal inclusion. The wide fracture area (Fig.  6 c) shows a crack region in the subsurface, surrounded by a rougher outer fracture area. The higher magnification SEM of the crack-initiation region (Region 1) reveals a roughly elliptical faceted area where the crack started around an inclusion. This area exhibits a delicate granular appearance (optically dark) and reflects extremely slow crack growth at the threshold of crack propagation. Notably, very little ductile behavior is seen in this interior region; instead, the fracture surface is flat and featureless on the scale of individual grains, a sign that the crack advanced in a quasi-brittle manner initially (likely along crystallographic planes or phase boundaries) when the stress intensity was very low. EDS analysis reveals a non-metallic inclusion at the origin; the inclusion particle spectra indicate a carbon-rich composition. One spot analysis measured an exceedingly high carbon content (on the order of 60–65 wt% C) with very low Ni (5–10%) and Ti (10–20%) and some oxygen (15–20%). Such a signature is characteristic of a titanium carbide inclusion, essentially TiC, which contains primarily Ti and C and almost no Ni. This strongly suggests that the crack in this sample originated from a TiC particle in the matrix. A nearby EDS spectrum in the same region showed slightly more oxygen (and corresponding lower carbon), implying that the carbide inclusion may have an oxide shell or there were near oxide inclusions as well.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: This work establishes a microstructure-based VHCF framework for a Ni-rich wrought NiTi SMAs by combining DSC, monotonic tension, 20 kHz pulse-pause ultrasonic fatigue (R =  − 1), and SEM/EDS fractography. The selected solutionizing (1000 °C/2 h) plus aging (600 °C/1 h) treatment suppressed transformation temperatures and introduced an intermediate R-phase on cooling, yielding A f  near 9–10 °C. Consistent with this calorimetric signature, room-temperature tension confirmed a fully austenitic starting state (E = 61.9 GPa) and a clear stress-induced martensitic transformation response with a SIMT onset near 223 MPa and a 250–300 MPa plateau. S–N data spanning 10 5  to 10 9  cycles follow a shallow stress-life trend (Basquin σ f ′ = 653.7 MPa, b = − 0.089) with increasing scatter at long lives and no evidence of an endurance limit within the tested range. Fractography reveals a stress-dependent shift in crack initiation: higher-amplitude failures are dominated by surface-initiated cracking associated with transformation-assisted slip/localization, whereas VHCF failures nucleate subsurface at rare, life-limiting Ti–rich inclusions. EDS consistently identifies carbon-rich TiC and oxidized Ti 2 NiO x  at or near crack origins in long-life failures, supporting an inclusion-controlled weakest-link mechanism as the cyclic driving force decreases.

The VHCF stress levels (e.g., ~ 100 MPa near 10 9  cycles) should be interpreted in the context of NiTi’s lower modulus and transformation-mediated response rather than compared directly to conventional structural alloys on stress amplitude alone; 100 MPa corresponds to an elastic strain amplitude of 0.14% for this material. The reported VHCF behavior is specific to the studied precipitation state and fully reversed loading; because NiTi fatigue is mean-stress/mean-strain sensitive, translation to service conditions requires additional VHCF datasets under representative mean loads. Finally, temperature rise was minimized via pulse-pause loading and forced-air cooling, but not directly instrumented, and oxygen-rich EDS signatures may reflect oxide-bearing inclusions and/or post-fracture oxidation. Future work will integrate in situ thermometry with inert-atmosphere ultrasonic testing, site-specific cross-sections, and inclusion statistics (including extreme-value analysis) to develop probabilistic VHCF design maps for NiTi.
